genZNote: Swims up your nose in warm lake water, not down your throat — the exact reason nose clips actually matter.

morphology.shape: Amoeboid trophozoite (infective form); transient flagellate form in water; cyst form under adverse conditions

habitat.naturalHabitat: Warm freshwater — lakes, rivers, hot springs, and poorly chlorinated or maintained swimming pools
habitat.hostAssociation: Free-living in the environment; humans are accidental hosts, not part of its normal life cycle
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Thrives in warm water (up to 45°C), with higher risk during hot summer months and periods of low water levels
habitat.reservoir: Warm natural and man-made freshwater bodies

microscopy.stain: Wet mount of CSF for motile trophozoites; trichrome stain
microscopy.appearance: Motile amoeboid trophozoites with characteristic slug-like directional movement

culture.media: Non-nutrient agar with an E. coli overlay (amoeba enrichment culture)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Grows and feeds on the bacterial lawn, forming visible trails
culture.colonyMorphology: Not applicable in the traditional sense — trophozoites are seen migrating across the agar surface

identificationClues: History of swimming/diving in warm freshwater (lakes, hot springs, poorly chlorinated pools) in the days before symptom onset
Motile trophozoites visible on wet mount of CSF, with characteristic amoeboid movement
Rapid onset of severe headache, fever, and meningitis-like symptoms progressing to coma, typically within about a week of exposure
Extremely high mortality (over 97%) despite treatment, reflecting how rapidly the disease progresses

diseases: Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) — a rapidly progressive, usually fatal CNS infection
virulenceFactors: Direct invasion via the nasal mucosa and cribriform plate, tracking along the olfactory nerve into the brain
Amoebic proteases (e.g., 'food cups' or amoebastomes) that lyse and phagocytose host neural tissue directly
clinicalImportance.transmission: Enters through the nasal mucosa during swimming, diving, or other activities that force warm freshwater up the nose (not via drinking contaminated water and not via person-to-person spread)
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Rare but almost always fatal; the vast majority of US cases occur in southern states during summer months in individuals swimming in warm freshwater lakes or rivers
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: A history of recent freshwater swimming combined with rapid-onset severe meningoencephalitis should prompt urgent CSF wet mount examination and PCR testing for Naegleria, since delay in treatment initiation is strongly associated with fatal outcome

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Not applicable — diagnosed by CSF wet mount/PCR
examFacts.importantDisease: Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) — nearly always fatal
examFacts.importantTest: CSF wet mount for motile trophozoites; PCR
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A thermophilic free-living amoeba that enters through the nose during warm-freshwater swimming and causes an almost universally fatal meningoencephalitis
